# What MLOps is {#sec-ch-ops-intro}

> *"It may be surprising to the academic community to know that only a tiny
> fraction of the code in many ML systems is actually devoted to learning or
> prediction."* — D. Sculley et al., 2015 [@sculley2015]

#| echo: false
import opsbook as ob

import json, hashlib, shutil

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- describe the **life cycle** of a machine-learning system and the roles of
  the people who build and run it, and say what makes it different from
  ordinary software;
- define and measure **prediction churn** between two versions of a model,
  and prove that it is bounded below by their difference in accuracy and
  above by the sum of their errors;
- recognise the main kinds of **technical debt** specific to ML systems —
  entanglement, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, glue code,
  configuration — and demonstrate entanglement in code;
- place a system on the **maturity** scales used in industry, and compute
  its **ML Test Score**, including the cheapest plan to raise it;
- find your way around the **tool stack** of MLOps, read a **model card**,
  write one, and download model files **pinned by revision and content hash**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
What MLOps is and why it exists; the roles of the ML engineer and of the data
scientist; maturity models for MLOps; the tools used across the life cycle;
working with a code-hosting platform and with a model hub.
:::

## From a model to a system {#sec-ops-lifecycle}

### The life cycle

A notebook that trains a classifier and prints its test accuracy answers one
question: *can* this problem be learnt from these data? A **system** answers
a different one, every second, for months: *what is the sentiment of this
post?* — for posts nobody has seen, arriving through a network, while the
people writing them, the code around the model and the model itself keep
changing. Between the two lies a cycle of activities, drawn in
@fig-ops-lifecycle:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-ops-lifecycle
%%| fig-cap: "The life cycle of an ML system. The inner loop (data → training → evaluation) is the one of Parts III and IV; MLOps adds the outer loop through deployment and monitoring back to the data, and the automation that makes it repeatable."
flowchart LR
  P[Problem<br/>and metrics] --> D[Data<br/>collection,<br/>labelling]
  D --> T[Training and<br/>experiments]
  T --> E[Evaluation<br/>and tests]
  E -->|not good enough| T
  E --> R[Registry:<br/>versioned model]
  R --> S[Deployment<br/>and serving]
  S --> M[Monitoring:<br/>service, data,<br/>predictions]
  M -->|drift, new data,<br/>new labels| D
  M -->|incident| S
```

1. **Problem and metrics** — what decision the model supports, how success is
   measured, what an error costs (@thm-cost-threshold showed how costs move
   the optimal threshold).
2. **Data** — collection, labelling, validation, versioning.
3. **Training and experiments** — many runs with different data, features,
   models and hyperparameters; each run must be recorded to be comparable
   and repeatable (@sec-ch-ops-repro).
4. **Evaluation and tests** — held-out metrics (@sec-classification-metrics),
   behavioural tests, comparison with the model in production
   (@sec-ch-ops-testing).
5. **Registry** — the chosen model, with its version, lineage and metadata,
   becomes an artefact that can be deployed and rolled back.
6. **Deployment and serving** — the model behind an API or in a batch job,
   packaged in a container, released gradually (@sec-ch-ops-serving,
   @sec-ch-ops-deploy).
7. **Monitoring** — of the service (latency, errors), of the inputs and of the
   predictions (drift), and of quality when labels arrive
   (@sec-ch-ops-monitor) — which feeds back into new data and new training
   runs, scheduled by an orchestrator (@sec-ch-ops-orch).

**MLOps** is the set of practices, roles and tools that make this cycle
reliable, repeatable and fast: the application to machine learning of the
ideas of DevOps — version everything, automate the path from a commit to
production, test at every step, observe what runs — extended to the two
artefacts that ordinary software does not have, **data** and **trained
models**. Kreuzberger, Kühl and Hirschl, after a literature review and
interviews with practitioners, define it as a paradigm spanning best
practices, concepts and a development culture for the end-to-end
conceptualisation, implementation, monitoring, deployment and scalability of
ML products, built on CI/CD, workflow orchestration, reproducibility,
versioning of data, models and code, collaboration, continuous training and
evaluation, metadata tracking and monitoring [@kreuzberger2023, §IV–V].

### Who does what

The cycle needs several skills, which organisations distribute over
different roles [@kreuzberger2023, §V.C]:

| Role | Main responsibility | Typical artefacts |
|---|---|---|
| **data scientist** | framing the problem, exploring data, choosing and evaluating models | analyses, experiments, a candidate model and its evaluation |
| **ML engineer** | turning the candidate into a dependable component: training pipelines, packaging, serving, tests, monitoring | pipelines, services, images, tests, dashboards |
| **data engineer** | getting data in and keeping it correct: ingestion, storage, transformations, quality checks | data pipelines, schemas, tables |
| **platform / DevOps engineer, SRE** | the infrastructure everything runs on: CI/CD, clusters, observability, on-call | runners, clusters, alerting |
| **domain expert, product owner** | what the model is for and what counts as good enough | requirements, labelling guidelines, acceptance criteria |

The line between data scientist and ML engineer is the one this part is about.
A data scientist optimises a metric on a dataset; an ML engineer is
responsible for that metric staying true when the dataset is replaced by the
world. In small teams one person plays every role — which is exactly the
situation of the project of this part.

### What is different about ML systems

Three properties set ML systems apart from the software of Parts I and II.

1. **Behaviour comes from data.** The logic of a classifier is not written
   by anyone; it is estimated. Changing the training data, or merely its
   order or the random seed, changes the logic — without any change in the
   code that a code review would see.
2. **Failures are silent.** A bug in ordinary code usually raises an
   exception or returns something visibly wrong. A model whose inputs have
   drifted keeps returning well-formed, confident, wrong answers. Detecting
   that needs statistics, not stack traces (@sec-ch-ops-monitor).
3. **Everything is coupled.** Sculley et al. call it the CACE principle:
   *changing anything changes everything* [@sculley2015, §2.1]. Inputs are
   not isolated: add a feature, drop a word from a vocabulary, change a
   regularisation constant, and every weight moves — so every prediction may
   move.

The simplest measurement of the first and third points is how many answers
change between two versions of a model.

::: {#def-ops-churn}
## Prediction churn
For two classifiers $f$ and $g$ and inputs $X$ drawn from a distribution
$\mathcal D$, the **churn** between them is
$$
C(f, g) = P_{X \sim \mathcal D}\bigl(f(X) \ne g(X)\bigr),
$$ {#eq-ops-churn}
estimated on a sample by the fraction of inputs on which their predictions
differ [@milanifard2016].
:::

Churn needs no labels. It is what users experience when a model is replaced:
the fraction of identical requests that now get a different answer. Its
relation to accuracy is simple and useful.

::: {#prp-ops-churn}
## Churn is sandwiched by accuracies
Let $\mathrm{err}(f) = P(f(X) \ne Y)$ and $\mathrm{acc}(f) = 1 -
\mathrm{err}(f)$, for $(X, Y) \sim \mathcal D$. Then
$$
\bigl|\mathrm{acc}(f) - \mathrm{acc}(g)\bigr| \;\le\; C(f, g) \;\le\;
\mathrm{err}(f) + \mathrm{err}(g).
$$ {#eq-ops-churn-bounds}
The same inequalities hold exactly for the empirical quantities on any finite
sample.
:::

*In one line:* two models can differ in accuracy only on inputs where they
disagree, and they can disagree only where at least one of them is wrong.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-churn
Write $A = \{f(X) = Y\}$ and $B = \{g(X) = Y\}$. Then $\mathrm{acc}(f) -
\mathrm{acc}(g) = P(A) - P(B) = P(A \setminus B) - P(B \setminus A)$, so
$|\mathrm{acc}(f) - \mathrm{acc}(g)| \le \max\{P(A \setminus B), P(B
\setminus A)\} \le P(A \setminus B) + P(B \setminus A)$. On $A \setminus B$
we have $f(X) = Y \ne g(X)$, and on $B \setminus A$ we have $g(X) = Y \ne
f(X)$: both are inside $\{f(X) \ne g(X)\}$ and disjoint, so their total
probability is at most $C(f, g)$. For the upper bound: if $f(X) \ne g(X)$
the two cannot both equal $Y$, so $\{f \ne g\} \subseteq A^c \cup B^c$ and
$C(f, g) \le P(A^c) + P(B^c) = \mathrm{err}(f) + \mathrm{err}(g)$. On a
finite sample, replace $P$ with the empirical distribution: every step is the
same. $\blacksquare$
:::

The lower bound says that two models with **the same accuracy** may still
churn a lot — up to the sum of their error rates. Let us measure it on the
synthetic posts of this part (introduced on the part's overview page): two
models trained on two samples of 3 000 posts from the *same* distribution,
compared on 5 000 fresh posts.

```{python}
posts = ob.make_posts(3, seed=0)
print(posts.to_string())
```

```{python}
test = ob.make_posts(5000, seed=100)
train_a = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=1)
train_b = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=2)            # same distribution, another sample
f = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
g = ob.train_model(train_b.text, train_b.label)

pf, pg = f.predict(test.text), g.predict(test.text)
acc_f, acc_g = accuracy_score(test.label, pf), accuracy_score(test.label, pg)
churn = np.mean(pf != pg)
print(f"accuracy f = {acc_f:.4f}, accuracy g = {acc_g:.4f}")
print(f"churn       = {churn:.4f}")
print(f"bounds      : {abs(acc_f - acc_g):.4f} <= {churn:.4f} <= {(1 - acc_f) + (1 - acc_g):.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
CHURN_PCT = f"{100 * churn:.1f}"
DIFF_PCT = f"{100 * abs(acc_f - acc_g):.1f}"
```

The two models differ in accuracy by `{python} DIFF_PCT` points, yet
`{python} CHURN_PCT` % of the posts get a different label from them. Nobody
changed a line of code: only the sample. Which posts flip? Mostly the
ambiguous ones, where both models are unsure:

```{python}
flipped = test[pf != pg].assign(f=pf[pf != pg], g=pg[pf != pg])
conf_all = f.predict_proba(test.text).max(axis=1)
print(f"mean confidence of f: all posts {conf_all.mean():.3f}, "
      f"flipped posts {conf_all[pf != pg].mean():.3f}")
print(flipped.head(6).to_string())
```

The mean confidence of the first model on the flipped posts is far below its
average: churn concentrates near the decision boundaries — and so does most
of the work of monitoring and testing later in the part.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops1-lifecycle-easy}
## Easy — churn by hand
Two sentiment models label ten posts whose true labels are
`[2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]`. Model $f$ predicts
`[2, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0]`, model $g$ predicts
`[2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 2]`. Compute both accuracies and the churn, and
check @eq-ops-churn-bounds. Then build, by hand, two predictors on these ten
posts with the **same** accuracy and the **largest possible** churn.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For the second part, the upper bound $\mathrm{err}(f) + \mathrm{err}(g)$ is
attained when the two models are never wrong on the same post.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
y10 = np.array([2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2])
f10 = np.array([2, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0])
g10 = np.array([2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 2])
acc = lambda p: np.mean(p == y10)
print(f"acc f = {acc(f10):.1f}, acc g = {acc(g10):.1f}, churn = {np.mean(f10 != g10):.1f}")
print(f"{abs(acc(f10) - acc(g10)):.1f} <= {np.mean(f10 != g10):.1f} <= {(1 - acc(f10)) + (1 - acc(g10)):.1f}")

# Same accuracy (0.7), wrong on disjoint posts: churn = 0.3 + 0.3
h1 = y10.copy(); h1[[0, 1, 2]] = (y10[[0, 1, 2]] + 1) % 3
h2 = y10.copy(); h2[[3, 4, 5]] = (y10[[3, 4, 5]] + 1) % 3
print(f"acc h1 = {acc(h1):.1f}, acc h2 = {acc(h2):.1f}, churn = {np.mean(h1 != h2):.1f}")
```
Both $f$ and $g$ have accuracy 0.7 but disagree on 4 posts out of 10: the
lower bound $|0.7 - 0.7| = 0$ is far from tight. Two models wrong on three
posts each, never the same ones, reach the upper bound $0.3 + 0.3 = 0.6$:
"same accuracy" says nothing about whether users see the same answers. A
frequent slip is to compare accuracies and conclude that a retrained model
"behaves the same".
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-lifecycle-medium}
## Medium — where does churn come from?
With the synthetic posts, separate the sources of churn: train pairs of models
that differ (a) only in the training sample (same size), (b) only in the
regularisation constant `C` (same sample), (c) only in the vocabulary (unigrams
versus uni- and bigrams). Measure the churn on 5 000 test posts for each, and
the accuracy of each model.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`ob.train_model` takes `C=` and `ngram=`; keep everything else fixed when you
change one factor. Logistic regression is fitted by a deterministic solver, so
the seed alone does not change it — the sample does.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def pair_churn(m1, m2):
    p1, p2 = m1.predict(test.text), m2.predict(test.text)
    return (np.mean(p1 != p2), accuracy_score(test.label, p1), accuracy_score(test.label, p2))

base = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
cases = {
    "(a) another sample":        ob.train_model(train_b.text, train_b.label),
    "(b) C = 0.5 instead of 4":  ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label, C=0.5),
    "(c) unigrams only":         ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label, ngram=(1, 1)),
}
for name, other in cases.items():
    c, a1, a2 = pair_churn(base, other)
    print(f"{name:26s} churn {c:.4f}   acc {a1:.4f} -> {a2:.4f}")
```
Each change alone flips some of the answers: a new sample about 2 %, a
stronger regularisation about 3 % (and costs two points of accuracy), the
loss of bigrams nearly 8 % (and six points). The vocabulary change (c) is the
one that changes what the model can *express*: without bigrams, "not great" and
"great" share their only informative feature. The typical mistake is to
change two things at once and attribute the churn to one of them.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-lifecycle-hard}
## Hard — should the retrained model replace the old one?
A model trained on 3 000 posts is in production. A month later, 3 000 newer
posts are available, in which the share of negative posts has grown to 45 %
and a few words have shifted polarity (`swap={"cheap": 0, "fast": 0}`).
Train a challenger on the new posts and compare it with the champion on a
fresh sample of the *new* distribution: accuracies, churn, and the posts whose
answer changes from right to wrong. Propose a rule, using churn and accuracy,
to decide whether to promote the challenger, and apply it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Split the churn into four kinds: right → right (impossible), right → wrong,
wrong → right, wrong → wrong (a different wrong label). The net gain in
accuracy is (wrong → right) − (right → wrong). A rule might require a
positive net gain *and* bound the right → wrong flips, which are the visible
regressions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
NEW = dict(prior=(0.45, 0.30, 0.25), swap={"cheap": 0, "fast": 0})
champion = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
new_train = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=21, **NEW)
challenger = ob.train_model(new_train.text, new_train.label)
new_test = ob.make_posts(5000, seed=22, **NEW)

y_new = new_test.label.to_numpy()
p_old, p_new = champion.predict(new_test.text), challenger.predict(new_test.text)
right_old, right_new = p_old == y_new, p_new == y_new
kinds = {
    "right -> wrong": np.mean(right_old & ~right_new),
    "wrong -> right": np.mean(~right_old & right_new),
    "wrong -> other wrong": np.mean(~right_old & ~right_new & (p_old != p_new)),
}
print(f"accuracy champion {right_old.mean():.4f}, challenger {right_new.mean():.4f}, "
      f"churn {np.mean(p_old != p_new):.4f}")
for k, v in kinds.items():
    print(f"  {k:22s} {v:.4f}")

def promote(gain, regressions, min_gain=0.01, max_regressions=0.02):
    """Promote if the net gain is at least 1 point and at most 2 % of answers regress."""
    return gain >= min_gain and regressions <= max_regressions

gain = right_new.mean() - right_old.mean()
print("net gain", round(gain, 4), "-> promote" if promote(gain, kinds["right -> wrong"]) else "-> keep champion")
```
The net gain equals "wrong → right" minus "right → wrong", as the proof of
@prp-ops-churn decomposes it. The challenger, trained on data that reflects
the new world, gains several points; the price is a smaller fraction of posts
that were right and become wrong. The thresholds in `promote` are a policy
choice, not a statistical test — @sec-ch-ops-cicd replaces "at least one
point" with a paired test that accounts for the sample size, and
@sec-ch-ops-orch with a cost model. Comparing the two models on the *old*
distribution would be the classic mistake: it measures how well the
challenger imitates the past.
:::

## Technical debt in ML systems {#sec-ops-debt}

### Debt that compounds

**Technical debt** is Ward Cunningham's metaphor for the future cost of a
shortcut taken now: like a loan, it buys speed today and charges interest on
every later change, until it is repaid by refactoring. Sculley et al. argued
that ML systems are unusually prone to it, because on top of the debt of
ordinary code they accumulate debt at the *system* level, which no code
review sees [@sculley2015]. Their catalogue, restated:

| Kind of debt | What it looks like | Remedy (chapter) |
|---|---|---|
| **entanglement (CACE)** | one change in data, features or hyperparameters moves every prediction | version and compare models, measure churn (@sec-ops-lifecycle), test behaviours (@sec-ch-ops-testing) |
| **correction cascades** | model B is trained to fix the output of model A; A can no longer be improved without breaking B | model A's output as an explicit, versioned interface |
| **undeclared consumers** | other systems silently read the model's outputs or logs | access through an API with a contract (@sec-ch-ops-serving) |
| **unstable data dependencies** | an input signal produced by another team changes meaning | data validation, versioned inputs (@sec-ch-ops-repro), drift monitoring (@sec-ch-ops-monitor) |
| **hidden feedback loops** | the model's decisions shape the data it will be retrained on | holdout traffic, logging of decisions (@sec-ch-ops-orch) |
| **glue code and pipeline jungles** | most of the code adapts formats between packages and scripts | reusable components, an orchestrated DAG (@sec-ch-ops-orch) |
| **dead experimental code paths** | flags for experiments that never ended | delete them; tests for configurations |
| **configuration debt** | more lines of configuration than of model code, unreviewed | configuration in version control, validated by schemas |
| **changes in the external world** | thresholds and assumptions that held at training time | monitoring and alerts (@sec-ch-ops-monitor) |

The rest of the part is a set of tools against these rows. One of them can
be seen at once in code.

### Entanglement, measured

```{python}
#| echo: false
N_FEAT = len(ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)[0].vocabulary_)
```

The model of this part has a few thousand features (`{python} N_FEAT` for the
first training sample): one per word and word pair. Suppose an engineer decides that emojis are noise and removes them from
the input. The posts *without* emojis are, apparently, untouched — their
features are the same. Are their predictions the same?

```{python}
import re
strip = lambda texts: [re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", "", t).strip() for t in texts]

with_emoji = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
without_emoji = ob.train_model(strip(train_a.text), train_a.label)

no_emoji = test[~test.text.str.contains(r"[^\w\s]", regex=True)]
p1 = with_emoji.predict(no_emoji.text)
p2 = without_emoji.predict(no_emoji.text)
prob_shift = np.abs(with_emoji.predict_proba(no_emoji.text) - without_emoji.predict_proba(no_emoji.text)).max(axis=1)
print(f"{len(no_emoji)} test posts contain no emoji")
print(f"churn on them: {np.mean(p1 != p2):.4f}; "
      f"median change of the largest class probability: {np.median(prob_shift):.4f}")
```

The predictions of posts that never contained an emoji change too — few of
them, `{python} f"{100 * np.mean(p1 != p2):.2f}"` %, but not zero, and almost
every probability moves a little. The reason is that the weights are estimated **jointly**: with an L2 penalty the
optimiser trades the weight of every feature against every other, and the
TF-IDF normalisation divides each post's vector by its length, so removing a
feature changes the scale of the others. No feature is an island — this is
CACE. The practical consequence is a rule of this part: *any* change to data,
features, preprocessing or hyperparameters produces a **new model version**,
evaluated and released as such.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops1-debt-easy}
## Easy — name the debt
For each situation, name the kind of debt from the table and the remedy.
(a) The marketing team reads the model's daily CSV of predictions from a
shared folder to build its own report. (b) A second model "corrects"
the first model's labels for posts about one product. (c) The production
service uses a different tokeniser from the training notebook. (d) A
`USE_EXPERIMENTAL_FEATURES` flag, last switched on two years ago, still
guards 300 lines of code. (e) The model is retrained every week on posts
that the previous model had flagged as negative and sent to human review.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Ask for each: who depends on what, and does anyone know? Does the model
influence its own future data? Is there code no one runs?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) **Undeclared consumer**: the CSV became an API without a contract; any
change of column or meaning breaks the report silently. Remedy: expose the
predictions through a documented, versioned interface and know who uses it.
(b) **Correction cascade**: improving the first model now changes the input
of the second. Remedy: train one model with the product as a feature, or make
the first model's output an explicit, versioned interface. (c) **Training–
serving skew**, a form of glue-code and unstable-dependency debt: the same
preprocessing must be one artefact — the scikit-learn pipeline of
`ob.train_model` stores vectoriser and classifier together precisely so that
the server cannot use another one. (d) **Dead experimental code path**:
delete it (version control remembers it). (e) **Hidden feedback loop**: only
posts the model already flagged get labels, so its errors on the other posts
are never corrected; @sec-ch-ops-orch simulates the effect and the remedy (a
random holdout sent to review regardless of the prediction).
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-debt-medium}
## Medium — how far does a change reach?
Measure the reach of a small vocabulary change: retrain the model ignoring
**one** word (`"recommend"`, by deleting it from the training and test
posts), and report the churn on the posts that do **not** contain that word.
Repeat for five different words and for a change of `C` from 4 to 3.5. Which
changes reach further?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Delete the word with a regular expression on word boundaries (`\bword\b`),
then compare the original and the retrained model on the same set of posts
that never contained it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def drop(texts, word):
    return [re.sub(rf"\b{word}\b", "", t).replace("  ", " ").strip() for t in texts]

base = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
for word in ["recommend", "rude", "today", "camera", "not"]:
    m = ob.train_model(drop(train_a.text, word), train_a.label)
    untouched = test[~test.text.str.contains(rf"\b{word}\b", regex=True)]
    c = np.mean(base.predict(untouched.text) != m.predict(untouched.text))
    print(f"without {word!r:12s} churn on {len(untouched):4d} posts without it: {c:.4f}")
m = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label, C=3.5)
print(f"C = 3.5 instead of 4     churn on all posts:                {np.mean(base.predict(test.text) != m.predict(test.text)):.4f}")
```
Removing a rare, mildly informative word moves few predictions; removing
`"not"` — the word that carries negation — reaches much further, even on posts
without it, because the weights of the polar words were estimated *together
with* it. A tiny change of the regularisation constant also changes answers.
A common mistake is to measure churn on all posts: the point of the exercise
is the change on inputs that the edit did not touch.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-debt-hard}
## Hard — a configuration that cannot lie
Configuration debt grows when settings live in several places (a notebook, a
script's defaults, environment variables) and nobody can say which values a
model was trained with. Design a small configuration object for the training
of the local model — vocabulary (`ngram`), `C`, data seed and size — that is
(i) validated (impossible values rejected), (ii) serialised canonically, and
(iii) identified by a hash, stored **inside** the trained model, so that a
model can always tell which configuration produced it. Show that two
configurations equal in content but written in a different order get the
same identifier.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
A frozen dataclass with checks in `__post_init__` is enough; a canonical JSON
(`sort_keys=True`, fixed separators) is the input of the hash. Attach the
hash to the fitted pipeline as an attribute, or save it next to it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TrainConfig:
    ngram_max: int = 2          # 1 = unigrams, 2 = uni + bigrams
    C: float = 4.0
    data_seed: int = 1
    n_train: int = 3000

    def __post_init__(self):    # (i) reject impossible values early
        if self.ngram_max not in (1, 2, 3):
            raise ValueError("ngram_max must be 1, 2 or 3")
        if not self.C > 0:
            raise ValueError("C must be positive")
        if self.n_train < 100:
            raise ValueError("at least 100 training posts")

    def canonical(self) -> str:  # (ii) one byte sequence per content
        return json.dumps(asdict(self), sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))

    @property
    def id(self) -> str:         # (iii) content identifier
        return ob.sha256(self.canonical())[:12]

def train(cfg: TrainConfig):
    data = ob.make_posts(cfg.n_train, seed=cfg.data_seed)
    model = ob.train_model(data.text, data.label, C=cfg.C, ngram=(1, cfg.ngram_max))
    model.config_ = cfg          # the model carries its configuration
    return model

c1 = TrainConfig(C=4.0, ngram_max=2)
c2 = TrainConfig(**json.loads('{"n_train": 3000, "data_seed": 1, "C": 4.0, "ngram_max": 2}'))
print(c1.canonical(), c1.id, c2.id, c1.id == c2.id)
m = train(c1)
print("model trained with config", m.config_.id)
try:
    TrainConfig(C=0)
except ValueError as e:
    print("rejected:", e)
```
The identifier depends on the content only, so a configuration read from a
file in another order is recognised as the same one; any change of value
gives another identifier (a collision would need the hash to collide,
@thm-ctr-collision). Storing the configuration inside the model makes the
artefact self-describing — @sec-ch-ops-repro extends the idea to data and
code. Typical mistakes: hashing `str(dict)` (its order depends on insertion),
and validating only when the value is used, hours into a run.
:::

## Maturity: levels and the ML Test Score {#sec-ops-maturity}

### Maturity levels

A **maturity model** is a ladder of levels describing how much of the life
cycle is automated and reliable. Two are widely quoted. Google's architecture
guide has three levels [@google2024mlops]:

- **level 0 — manual process**: data analysis, training and validation are
  run by hand (often in notebooks); the model is handed over to be deployed;
  releases are rare; no monitoring;
- **level 1 — ML pipeline automation**: the training pipeline is automated,
  so the model is retrained in production on new data (**continuous
  training**), with automated data and model validation, a feature store and
  metadata; the pipeline itself is still deployed by hand;
- **level 2 — CI/CD pipeline automation**: changes to the *pipeline code* are
  built, tested and deployed automatically, so that new ideas reach
  production as fast as new data do.

Microsoft's model has five levels, from **0 — no MLOps** through **1 —
DevOps but no MLOps** (application releases automated, models still handed
over), **2 — automated training**, **3 — automated model deployment**, to
**4 — full MLOps automated operations**, where monitoring can trigger
retraining and promotion [@microsoft2024maturity]. The two ladders say the
same thing with different granularity: the first step automates *training*,
the next automates the path to *production*, the last closes the loop from
*monitoring* back to training. They are qualitative; Breck et al. proposed a
number.

### The ML Test Score

Breck et al. collected, from experience with production systems at Google,
**28 tests and monitoring practices** in four sections of seven — **data**,
**model**, **ML infrastructure**, **monitoring** — and a rubric to score a
system [@breck2017]:

::: {#def-ops-mltestscore}
## ML Test Score
Each test earns **0** points if not done, **½** point if done manually with
the results documented and shared, **1** point if automated and run
repeatedly. The score of a section is the sum of its tests' points (between 0
and 7). The **ML Test Score** of the system is the **minimum** of the four
section scores.
:::

The minimum is deliberate: a system with perfect data tests and no monitoring
is as fragile as its weakest side. The paper reads the score roughly as: 0 —
a research project rather than a production system; up to 1 — not untested,
but probably with serious holes; up to 2 — a first pass at productionisation;
up to 3 — reasonably tested, with room for more automation; up to 5 — strong
automated testing and monitoring, fit for critical systems; above 5 —
exceptional [@breck2017, §VI]. One consequence of the minimum shapes any plan
to improve.

::: {#prp-ops-mltestscore}
## Raising the minimum decomposes by section
(i) The score is at least $s$ if and only if every section scores at least
$s$; improving a section that is already at or above $s$ does not help reach
$s$. (ii) If test $t$ of section $k$ costs $c_t$ to bring from its current
points to $1$, the cheapest way to reach score $s$ costs
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{4} \mathrm{cost}_k(s),
$$ {#eq-ops-mts-cost}
where $\mathrm{cost}_k(s)$ is the cheapest way to raise section $k$ alone to
$s$ — the four problems can be solved separately.
:::

*In one line:* with a minimum, only the weakest sections matter, and each of
them can be fixed on its own budget.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-mltestscore
(i) $\min_k S_k \ge s \iff S_k \ge s$ for every $k$, by definition of the
minimum; a section with $S_k \ge s$ imposes no constraint. (ii) A plan is a
set of tests to upgrade; its cost is the sum of their costs, which splits as
a sum over sections of the cost of the tests chosen in each. By (i) the plan
reaches $s$ if and only if, for every $k$, the tests chosen in section $k$
raise it to $s$ — a condition involving section $k$ only. The constraints
and the cost are therefore separable, and the minimum of a separable sum
over a product of independent choice sets is the sum of the minima.
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
SECTIONS = ["data", "model", "infrastructure", "monitoring"]

def ml_test_score(points: dict[str, list[float]]) -> tuple[float, dict]:
    """points[section] = seven values in {0, 0.5, 1}; returns (score, section sums)."""
    sums = {k: float(sum(v)) for k, v in points.items()}
    return min(sums.values()), sums

example = {                      # a typical "notebook in production" system
    "data":           [1, 0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, 0, 0],
    "model":          [1, 1, 0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0],
    "infrastructure": [1, 1, 1, 0.5, 0, 0, 0],
    "monitoring":     [0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
}
score, sums = ml_test_score(example)
print(sums, "-> ML Test Score", score)
```

Three good sections and an almost absent monitoring: the score is ½. By
@prp-ops-mltestscore, the next improvement must come from monitoring, whatever
the other sections do.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops1-maturity-easy}
## Easy — score a system
A team runs these practices. Data: a schema check is automated, feature
distributions are compared by hand once per release and documented, nothing
else. Model: the model is compared with a baseline by an automated test, and
hyperparameters were tuned by hand with documented results. Infrastructure:
training is reproducible by an automated script, the model is tested in a
staging environment by hand. Monitoring: latency and errors are alerted on
automatically, prediction distributions are inspected by hand every week.
Compute the section scores, the ML Test Score, and say at which level of
Google's ladder the team is.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Automated = 1, manual and documented = ½. The final score is the minimum,
not the mean.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
team = {"data": [1, 0.5], "model": [1, 0.5], "infrastructure": [1, 0.5], "monitoring": [1, 0.5]}
print(ml_test_score(team))
```
Every section scores 1.5, so the ML Test Score is 1.5: a first pass at
productionisation. Training is scripted but deployment and comparisons with
production are manual: closest to Google's **level 0**, on the way to level 1
(the next step is a training pipeline that runs on new data with automated
validation). Averaging the sections would give the same number here, but only
because they happen to be balanced.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-maturity-medium}
## Medium — the cheapest plan
Write a function that, given for each section the current points of its seven
tests and the cost of bringing each test to 1 point, finds the cheapest set of
upgrades that reaches a target score $s$. Use @prp-ops-mltestscore to solve the
sections separately, and check the result against a brute-force search over
all sets of upgrades on a small instance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Within one section, the problem is a small knapsack: choose a subset of tests
whose gains $1 - p_t$ add up to at least $s - S_k$, at minimum cost. With
seven tests, $2^7 = 128$ subsets per section can be enumerated; brute force
over all four sections at once is $2^{28}$ — too many — so check it on two
sections of four tests.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from itertools import combinations, product

def section_plan(points, costs, target):
    """Cheapest subset of tests raising sum(points) to >= target (exhaustive, 2^n subsets)."""
    best = (0.0, ()) if sum(points) >= target else (np.inf, None)
    n = len(points)
    for r in range(1, n + 1):
        for subset in combinations(range(n), r):
            gain = sum(1 - points[i] for i in subset)
            cost = sum(costs[i] for i in subset)
            if sum(points) + gain >= target - 1e-12 and cost < best[0]:
                best = (cost, subset)
    return best

def plan(points, costs, target):
    parts = {k: section_plan(points[k], costs[k], target) for k in points}
    return sum(c for c, _ in parts.values()), parts

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
pts = {k: [float(p) for p in rng.choice([0, 0.5, 1], size=4)] for k in ["data", "monitoring"]}
cst = {k: [int(c) for c in rng.integers(1, 10, size=4)] for k in pts}
total, parts = plan(pts, cst, target=3.0)

# brute force over all pairs of subsets of the two sections
brute = np.inf
for sa, sb in product(*[[s for r in range(5) for s in combinations(range(4), r)]] * 2):
    ok = all(sum(pts[k]) + sum(1 - pts[k][i] for i in s) >= 3.0 for k, s in zip(pts, (sa, sb)))
    if ok:
        brute = min(brute, sum(cst["data"][i] for i in sa) + sum(cst["monitoring"][i] for i in sb))
print("points", pts, "\ncosts", cst)
print("separable plan:", total, {k: v[1] for k, v in parts.items()}, "| brute force:", brute)
```
The separable plan and the brute force agree, as @eq-ops-mts-cost predicts,
and the separable search is exponentially cheaper ($4 \cdot 2^7$ subsets
instead of $2^{28}$). A typical mistake is a greedy choice by cost per point
across sections: it can spend budget on a section that is already above the
target.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-maturity-hard}
## Hard — a maturity plan for a sentiment service
You must bring the local sentiment model of this part to production. List,
for each of the four sections of the ML Test Score, the practices you would
implement, which chapter of this part teaches each, whether it would be manual
(½) or automated (1) in a first version, and the resulting score. Then say
which single addition would raise the score most, and why.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Think of the service of @sec-ch-ops-serving, the tests of
@sec-ch-ops-testing, the pipeline of @sec-ch-ops-cicd, the monitors of
@sec-ch-ops-monitor. Be honest about what a first version automates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
first_version = {
    "data": {"schema and length checks on inputs (ch. 3)": 1,
             "training data versioned by hash (ch. 2)": 1,
             "feature/label distributions compared with a reference (ch. 7)": 0.5},
    "model": {"behavioural tests: invariance and direction (ch. 4)": 1,
              "comparison with the production model by a paired test (ch. 6)": 1,
              "accuracy test sized for its false-failure rate (ch. 4)": 1,
              "calibration checked (ch. 3)": 0.5},
    "infrastructure": {"reproducible training, pinned environment (ch. 2)": 1,
                       "CI runs lint and tests on every push (ch. 6)": 1,
                       "image built and smoke-tested in CI (ch. 5-6)": 1,
                       "staged release with rollback (ch. 5)": 0.5},
    "monitoring": {"latency, errors, traffic alerts (ch. 7)": 1,
                   "input length and unknown-word rate monitored (ch. 7)": 1,
                   "predicted-class distribution drift (ch. 7)": 1,
                   "label-shift estimate without labels (ch. 7)": 0.5},
}
sums = {k: sum(v.values()) for k, v in first_version.items()}
print(sums, "-> ML Test Score", min(sums.values()))
```
With these choices the minimum is the data section (2.5), the only one
below 3: by
@prp-ops-mltestscore, the most valuable single addition is a data test — for
example automating the comparison of input distributions with the training
reference (½ → 1) or adding a test that the training data contain no
duplicates of evaluation posts (leakage, @sec-leakage). Adding a fifth
monitoring practice would leave the score unchanged. The mistake to avoid is
counting a dashboard someone *could* look at as a monitoring test: the rubric
asks for alerts or documented, repeated checks.
:::

## The tool stack, hubs and model cards {#sec-ops-stack}

### A map of the tools

Every step of the life cycle has tools; their landscape changes every year,
but the categories are stable. The ones used in this part are open-source and
run on a laptop:

| Need | What the tool does | Used in this part |
|---|---|---|
| isolated, pinned environments | one interpreter and set of packages per project | `venv`, `pip` with hashes (@sec-ch-ops-repro) |
| version control | history of code and configuration, collaboration | Git, GitHub |
| data and model versioning | content-addressed storage of large files | hashes and a small registry; Git LFS, DVC as alternatives |
| experiment tracking and registry | parameters, metrics, artefacts of runs; named model versions | MLflow (@sec-ch-ops-repro) |
| serving | an HTTP API in front of the model | FastAPI, uvicorn (@sec-ch-ops-serving) |
| testing and code quality | tests, linting, formatting | pytest, Ruff (@sec-ch-ops-testing) |
| packaging and deployment | images, containers, clusters | Docker, Kubernetes (@sec-ch-ops-deploy, Part V) |
| CI/CD | automated checks, builds and releases on every change | GitHub Actions (@sec-ch-ops-cicd) |
| monitoring | metrics, dashboards, alerts | Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager (@sec-ch-ops-monitor) |
| orchestration | scheduled DAGs of tasks with retries | Apache Airflow (@sec-ch-ops-orch) |
| model hubs | sharing pre-trained models with their documentation | Hugging Face Hub |

Two platforms recur. **GitHub** hosts Git repositories with pull requests,
issues, the **Actions** CI/CD service, a container registry, and
**Codespaces** — development environments in the cloud, defined by a
`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` file in the repository that names an image
and the tools to install, so that every contributor starts from the same
environment [@devcontainers2025]. **Hugging Face Hub** hosts models, datasets
and small demo applications (*Spaces*) as Git repositories: a model is a
repository with weights, configuration, tokenizer files and a `README.md`
that is its **model card** [@huggingface2026hub].

### Pinning what you download

A model on a hub is a moving target: its owner can push new weights to the
same name. Two identifiers make a download reproducible:

- the **revision** — a Git commit hash of the model repository — fixes *which
  version* of every file;
- the **content hash** of each file fixes *which bytes*: large files are
  stored through Git LFS, whose pointer files record the SHA-256 of the
  content [@gitlfs2024spec], and a downloader can verify it.

A download pinned by revision and checked by hash either gives exactly the
bytes that were tested, or fails loudly. The same idea — content addresses —
identifies image layers (@prp-ctr-merkle) and, in @sec-ch-ops-repro, Git
objects and model versions.

### Model cards and datasheets

Mitchell et al. proposed that every released model come with a short document,
the **model card**, stating what the model is, how it was trained and
evaluated, and where it should *not* be used [@mitchell2019]. Their sections:
model details (who, when, version, type, licence, citation); intended use and
out-of-scope uses; factors (groups, environments, instruments that affect
performance); metrics; evaluation data; training data; quantitative analyses
(disaggregated by factor); ethical considerations; caveats and
recommendations. **Datasheets for datasets** do the same for data: motivation,
composition, collection process, preprocessing, uses, distribution,
maintenance [@gebru2021]. On the Hugging Face Hub the card is the repository's
`README.md`, with a YAML header of machine-readable metadata (licence,
languages, datasets, tags) [@huggingface2026hub].

The project of this part starts from a public model card. Its main facts, as
published: the model is a RoBERTa-base [@liu2019roberta] further pre-trained
on about 124 million tweets from January 2018 to December 2021 and fine-tuned
for sentiment on the TweetEval benchmark [@barbieri2020]; it is described in
the TimeLMs paper [@loureiro2022] and integrated in the TweetNLP library
[@camachocollados2022]; its labels are 0 = negative, 1 = neutral,
2 = positive; it is meant for English; it is released under the CC BY 4.0
licence [@cardiffnlp2022card]. The card is short: it says little about
evaluation by group, about irony, or about how the model behaves on text that
is not a tweet — gaps that the project's own card must fill.

A model card can be generated from the evaluation itself, so that its numbers
cannot drift away from the model's. For the local model:

```{python}
card_model = ob.train_model(train_a.text, train_a.label)
report = classification_report(test.label, card_model.predict(test.text),
                               target_names=ob.LABELS, output_dict=True)

def model_card(model, report, train, config) -> str:
    rows = "\n".join(f"| {c} | {report[c]['precision']:.3f} | {report[c]['recall']:.3f} | "
                     f"{report[c]['f1-score']:.3f} | {int(report[c]['support'])} |" for c in ob.LABELS)
    return f"""---
license: cc-by-4.0
language: [en]
tags: [text-classification, sentiment]
---
# Local sentiment model (TF-IDF + logistic regression)

**Model details.** {config}. Trained on {len(train)} synthetic posts
(generator `opsbook.make_posts`, seed 1). Labels: 0 negative, 1 neutral, 2 positive.

**Intended use.** Teaching examples of Part VII. **Out of scope:** any real text.

**Evaluation** (5 000 synthetic posts from the training distribution, accuracy {report['accuracy']:.3f}):

| class | precision | recall | F1 | support |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{rows}

**Caveats.** Bag of words and word pairs: negation is captured only
inside adjacent pairs; unseen words are ignored; no calibration check yet.
"""

card = model_card(card_model, report, train_a, "TF-IDF (1-2-grams) + logistic regression, C = 4")
print(card)
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops1-stack-easy}
## Easy — read a model card
From the facts of the project model's card summarised above, answer: (a) What
input does the model expect, and in which language? (b) How must the
integer output be mapped to a sentiment? (c) Can the model be redistributed,
and on which condition? (d) Name two questions an operator would want
answered that the card does not answer, and which section of Mitchell et al.'s
template they belong to.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For (c), recall what the "BY" in CC BY means. For (d), think of who writes the
posts the service will see, and what the card says about evaluation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) English tweets — short social-media texts, written between 2018 and 2021
for the pre-training data. (b) 0 → negative, 1 → neutral, 2 → positive; the
service must apply this mapping, and a test should check it
(@sec-ch-ops-testing). (c) Yes: CC BY 4.0 allows copying, redistribution and
adaptation, commercially too, provided the authors are credited (attribution,
a link to the licence, and an indication of changes). (d) For instance: how
accurate is the model on posts written after 2021 or on other platforms
(*evaluation data*, *quantitative analyses*); how does it perform by topic,
dialect or for ironic posts (*factors*); what it should not be used for
(*intended use*). The typical mistake is to treat the card's benchmark score
as the accuracy the service will have on its own traffic.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-stack-medium}
## Medium — a card that stays true
Extend `model_card` so that it also reports (i) the accuracy on a sample with
the class priors changed to `(0.6, 0.2, 0.2)`, and (ii) the accuracy on posts
with slang (`slang_rate=1.0`), as "factors" in Mitchell et al.'s sense, and
writes the card next to the saved model with the SHA-256 of the model file in
it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Save the model with `joblib.dump` into a temporary folder first, hash the
file with `ob.sha256(path)`, then write `README.md` in the same folder.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import joblib

def factors(model) -> str:
    rows = []
    for name, kw in [("training distribution", {}), ("class priors 0.6 / 0.2 / 0.2", {"prior": (0.6, 0.2, 0.2)}),
                     ("every post with unseen slang", {"slang_rate": 1.0})]:
        d = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=7, **kw)
        rows.append(f"| {name} | {accuracy_score(d.label, model.predict(d.text)):.3f} |")
    return "| factor | accuracy |\n|---|---|\n" + "\n".join(rows)

folder = ob.project("card_demo")
joblib.dump(card_model, folder / "model.joblib")
digest = ob.sha256(folder / "model.joblib")
(folder / "README.md").write_text(card + "\n**Factors.**\n\n" + factors(card_model)
                                  + f"\n\n**Artefact.** `model.joblib`, SHA-256 `{digest[:16]}…`\n")
print((folder / "README.md").read_text().split("**Factors.**")[1])
```
The card now says, from measurements, that the class mix barely matters here
while unseen slang costs a little — and it names the exact bytes it describes.
Generating the card in the same run that saves the model is what keeps the two
consistent; hand-edited cards drift. A typical mistake is to hash the model
object in memory (its pickle can vary between runs and versions) instead of
the file actually shipped.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-stack-hard}
## Hard — a pinned downloader
Simulate a model hub with a local folder: a repository has revisions (commit
ids), each mapping file names to contents. Write
`download(repo, filename, revision, sha256, cache)` that (i) returns the
cached file if a file with that content hash is already cached, (ii)
otherwise fetches the file at that revision, verifies its SHA-256 and stores
it in the cache under its hash, and (iii) refuses a file whose hash does not
match. Show a second call served from the cache, a new revision of the same
file name not being picked up, and a tampered file being rejected.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Store cached files as `cache/<sha256>`: the name *is* the check. Write the
file under a temporary name and rename it only after verification, so an
interrupted download never leaves a wrong file under a right name
(@sec-atomic-writes).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
hub = ob.project("hub")
def publish(repo, revision, files):
    for name, content in files.items():
        ob.write(f"{repo}/{revision}/{name}", content, base=hub)

publish("acme/sentiment", "a1b2c3", {"config.json": '{"labels": ["negative", "neutral", "positive"]}'})
publish("acme/sentiment", "d4e5f6", {"config.json": '{"labels": ["neg", "neu", "pos"]}'})

class HashMismatch(Exception):
    pass

def download(repo, filename, revision, sha256, cache: Path) -> tuple[Path, str]:
    cache.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    target = cache / sha256
    if target.exists():                                   # (i) content already here
        return target, "cache"
    data = (hub / repo / revision / filename).read_bytes()   # (ii) "network" fetch
    if hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() != sha256:         # (iii) verify before keeping
        raise HashMismatch(f"{repo}@{revision}/{filename}")
    tmp = cache / (sha256 + ".part")
    tmp.write_bytes(data)
    tmp.replace(target)                                    # atomic rename
    return target, "hub"

cache = ob.project("cache")
expected = ob.sha256((hub / "acme/sentiment/a1b2c3/config.json").read_text())
for _ in range(2):
    path, origin = download("acme/sentiment", "config.json", "a1b2c3", expected, cache)
    print(origin, path.read_text().strip())
publish("acme/sentiment", "a1b2c3", {"config.json": '{"labels": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"]}'})  # tampering
shutil.rmtree(cache)
try:
    download("acme/sentiment", "config.json", "a1b2c3", expected, cache)
except HashMismatch as e:
    print("rejected:", e)
```
The second call is served from the cache because the content address is
known; the new revision `d4e5f6` is never seen because the revision is pinned;
and when the bytes behind a pinned revision change — here by tampering, in
reality by a corrupted transfer or a rewritten history — the hash check
refuses them. Note the tampered labels: swapping the order of two class names
would silently invert the meaning of every prediction. Typical mistakes: pinning
the revision but not checking the content, or checking it after the file has
been moved into its final place.
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The project starts from a pre-trained model on a hub, so
its first decisions belong to this chapter: pin the model by revision and
check its files by SHA-256 (@exr-ops1-stack-hard); write the project's own
model card, starting from the published one and adding what an operator needs
— the evaluation on the project's data, the label mapping, limits (English,
tweets of 2018–2021, irony, other platforms); compute an honest ML Test Score
of the delivery and say which section is weakest (@exr-ops1-maturity-hard);
and, when the model is retrained, measure the churn against the version in
production before promoting it (@exr-ops1-lifecycle-hard).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **"Same accuracy, same model"**: two versions with equal accuracy can
  disagree on many inputs (@prp-ops-churn). Measure churn.
- **Changing two things at once**: with entanglement, the effect of each
  change cannot be separated afterwards.
- **Training–serving skew**: preprocessing reimplemented in the service.
  Ship one artefact containing preprocessing and model.
- **Undeclared consumers** of predictions, logs or files.
- **Averaging the ML Test Score**: it is a minimum on purpose.
- **Downloading by name**: a model name is not a version. Pin the revision
  and verify content hashes.
- **Trusting a benchmark score** as the accuracy on your own traffic.
:::

## Summary

- An ML system is code + data + model + configuration + infrastructure; its
  life cycle closes a loop from monitoring back to data. MLOps applies
  DevOps practices to that loop, adding versioning and testing of data and
  models, continuous training, and monitoring of predictions.
- Retraining changes answers even when accuracy does not: churn satisfies
  $|\mathrm{acc}(f) - \mathrm{acc}(g)| \le C(f, g) \le \mathrm{err}(f) +
  \mathrm{err}(g)$ and concentrates on low-confidence inputs.
- ML systems accumulate system-level technical debt: entanglement (CACE),
  correction cascades, undeclared consumers, unstable data dependencies,
  feedback loops, glue code, configuration debt.
- Maturity ladders (Google 0–2, Microsoft 0–4) describe how much of the loop
  is automated; the ML Test Score is the minimum over four sections of 0/½/1
  points, and the cheapest plan to raise it decomposes by section.
- Hubs distribute models as repositories with model cards; reproducible use
  pins the revision and verifies content hashes.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ops1-churn-confidence}
**Churn and confidence.** Using two models trained on different samples (as in
@sec-ops-lifecycle), group the test posts into ten bins by the first model's
confidence (largest predicted probability) and plot the churn in each bin.
Then propose a rule that predicts which posts will change answer when the
model is retrained, and measure its precision.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| label: fig-ops-churn-confidence
#| fig-cap: "Churn between two models trained on different samples of the same distribution, by the first model's confidence. Answers change almost only where the model is unsure."
conf = f.predict_proba(test.text).max(axis=1)
bins = np.quantile(conf, np.linspace(0, 1, 11))
idx = np.clip(np.digitize(conf, bins[1:-1]), 0, 9)
rates = [np.mean((pf != pg)[idx == b]) for b in range(10)]
mids = [np.mean(conf[idx == b]) for b in range(10)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(mids, rates, marker="o", color=ob.COLORS[0])
ax.set_xlabel("confidence of model f (decile mean)")
ax.set_ylabel("churn in the decile")
plt.show()

rule = conf < np.quantile(conf, 0.2)            # "the 20 % least confident posts will flip"
print(f"precision of the rule {np.mean((pf != pg)[rule]):.3f}, "
      f"share of all flips it catches {np.sum((pf != pg) & rule) / np.sum(pf != pg):.3f}")
```
Churn falls steeply with confidence. Flagging the least confident fifth of
the posts catches most of the flips with a precision several times the base
churn rate: low-confidence inputs are where retraining, and drift, show
first — a reason to monitor the confidence distribution (@sec-ch-ops-monitor).
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-debt-feedback}
**A loop in miniature.** A service hides posts it predicts as negative, and
labels for retraining are collected only on the posts that remain visible.
Explain, without code, why the next model's estimated share of negative posts
will be biased, in which direction, and what minimal change in the data
collection removes the bias.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The training data of the next model are a sample selected by the current
model: posts predicted negative are missing, so negative posts are
under-represented — those that remain are mostly the current model's false
negatives, labelled correctly but few. The next model learns a lower prior
for the negative class and, through its intercept, predicts it less often,
which hides even fewer posts next time, and so on: a self-reinforcing loop.
The minimal fix is a **random holdout**: a small fraction of posts is shown
(or labelled) regardless of the prediction, giving an unbiased sample of the
traffic on which priors and accuracy can be estimated. @sec-ch-ops-orch
simulates such a loop.
:::

::: {#exr-ops1-card-review}
**Review a card.** Take the model card generated in @sec-ops-stack and check
it against Mitchell et al.'s nine sections: which are present, which are
missing, and what would you need to *measure* (not just write) to fill each
missing one for the local model?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Present: model details (type, configuration, labels, licence), intended use
and out-of-scope use, metrics and evaluation data (per-class precision,
recall, F1 on a stated sample), training data (size, generator, seed),
caveats. Missing or thin: **factors** and **quantitative analyses** —
performance disaggregated by topic, by post length, by presence of negation or
slang, which needs evaluation sets built per factor (@exr-ops1-stack-medium
started this); **ethical considerations** — for synthetic data, little, but
for real posts the risks of misclassifying dialects or minority languages;
**metrics** could add calibration (@sec-ch-ops-serving) and the uncertainty of
each number (an interval, @sec-ch-ops-testing). Writing these sections without
measuring them would turn the card into marketing.
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @sculley2015 — the technical-debt catalogue (§2–8); short and still the best
  first read on why ML systems are hard to maintain.
- @kreuzberger2023 — a definition of MLOps from a literature review and
  interviews: principles (§IV), components and roles (§V), architecture (§VI).
- @amershi2019 — nine stages of the ML workflow at Microsoft and the
  challenges teams report at each; @paleyes2022 — a survey of deployment case
  studies organised by stage of the life cycle.
- @breck2017 — the 28 tests and the scoring rubric (§II–VI); a checklist worth
  keeping next to every project.
- @google2024mlops and @microsoft2024maturity — the two maturity ladders,
  with the characteristics of each level.
- @milanifard2016 — prediction churn and methods to reduce it when models are
  retrained.
- @mitchell2019 and @gebru2021 — model cards and datasheets; @huggingface2026hub
  for how cards and metadata work on the Hub.
- @liu2019roberta, @barbieri2020, @loureiro2022 and @camachocollados2022 — the
  model family, benchmark and libraries behind the project's model.
